Posted May 11, 2001
(MarijuanaNews note: As a libertarian, I had long admired the editorial page of the Wall Street Journal. So I have been greatly saddened by its persistent support of the Drug War in a complete betrayal of its own principles.
See
Nahas versus Kassirer Fraud on Wall Street: How The Wall Street Journal defrauded the readers of its editorial page.

As noted in the excerpt -- immediately below – they claim their editorial philosophy is based on " the mantra ‘free markets and free people.’ " Contrast that with their recent editorial – second item below – which attacks a Dutch city for proposing drive-through cannabis stores, and then lies about the Dutch drugs policies.)

From http://opinionjournal.com/about/philosophy.html

Our Philosophy

Friday, July 28, 2000 12:01 a.m.

The Wall Street Journal has a long and proud tradition of vigorous and independent editorial commentary….

Looking back over this history, the surprise is not the change of views over the years but the constancy of them. They are united by the mantra " free markets and free people, " the principles, if you will, marked in the watershed year of 1776 by Thomas Jefferson's Declaration of Independence and Adam Smith's " Wealth of Nations. " So over the past century and into the next, the Journal stands for free trade and sound money. Against the interference of taxes and ukases by kings and other collectivists. For the defense of individual autonomy against dictators, bullies and even the tempers of momentary majorities. If these principles sound unexceptionable in theory, applying them to current issues is often unfashionable and controversial….

That is, we are guided by the tradition of free people, free markets set out by Charles Dow and elaborated by a long string of editors since….

Indeed, we believe that the ultimate function of the editorial pages is the same as the rest of the newspaper, to inform. But in opinion journalism we try to inform on questions to which there is no ultimate ascertainable truth--which is to say, the most interesting questions of life and society. We certainly offer our opinions as something we believe, but we do not offer them as the truth. We recognize that others may disagree, but see little value in equivocation. We hope that in stating our own views forcefully we raise and sharpen the level of debate and knowledge. And we hope that our editorials reflect not merely the passing whim of passing editors, but a body of thought shaped by a century of tradition.

(MarijuanaNews note: Venlo is a small city in south-eastern Netherlands, near the German border, with a population of around 70,000. They have a problem common in a number of Dutch border towns, too many young people coming across the border – in this case from Germany – just to buy some cannabis, which they cannot legally get at home. Their solution is to open a few drive-through cannabis stores on the edge of the city so the young Germans can buy their cannabis and go home. [The Dutch/German border has no check points.]

The city’s coffee-shops, located in the heart of the town are primarily for residents, and most small European cities are not designed for heavy traffic. [Citizens of other EU countries cannot be discriminated against, so the Dutch cannot exclude them from the coffee-shops.]

When the Belgians recently announced that they were going to tolerate cannabis possession and growing for personal use, but not sales, they even said that Belgians could go across the border to The Netherlands to buy Nederwiet, Dutch weed.

Tourism is a huge business in The Netherlands, and the Dutch are a friendly people, and the Venlo spokesperson made very clear that they did not have a problem with these cannabis buyers. Rather the problems come from the street hustlers, who pursue the young Germans, sometimes offering hard drugs, which the coffee shops do not sell.

This creates an atmosphere that offends the locals in small towns. Of course, in big cities like Amsterdam and Rotterdam, this is not considered a problem, but there the tourists are usually spending more time and money in other places as well.

In addition to the factual errors -- actually there are very few specifics offered – the most striking thing about the editorial is the snide tone of moral superiority. If DEAland cannabis policies were a great success, then this might be justifiable, but even after 13 million marijuana arrests DEAland has a higher rate of all drug use than does The Netherlands. Of course, there is no mention of arrests in the editorial. Prohibition is the one government program for which the Journal never counts the costs or measures the success.)

Drive-Thru Highs Take a Trip to Venlo, Holland, the World's Dopiest City.
From http://opinionjournal.com/editorial/feature.html?id=95000444

Dude!

That--or whatever is said these days simultaneously to express surprise, approval and joy--is one way to react to news that the town of Venlo, Holland, will soon be licensing drive-thru pot shops. Venlo, according to reports, is overflowing with drug tourists (most of them from nearby Germany) whose needs can no longer be met by its five licensed marijuana- and hashish-selling " coffee shops. " So the idea is to set up these drive-thrus just outside the city limits, cater efficiently to the clientele, and see them off on their merry way. Simplicity itself, right?

More like stupidity itself. But this gets us on the subject of drug legalization, about which the editorial position of this newspaper is tres uncool. Read on.
(MarijuanaNews note: Above, in their editorial philosophy, they say that standing " For the defense of individual autonomy against dictators, bullies and even the tempers of momentary majorities... is often unfashionable and controversial…. Now are they " unfashionable " for opposing majoritarian tyranny, or are they " uncool " for supporting it?)

As it turns out, in conceiving the idea of the drive-thrus, the city fathers of Venlo were not just adjusting supply to demand. Rather, says town spokeswoman Tamira Hankman, they were responding to " an environment that generally makes ordinary people feel unsafe. "

That means not only raffish drug tourists, but what these tourists bring in their wake: dealers peddling harder drugs, burglars, prostitutes, pimps and violent criminals.
(MarijuanaNews note: When did young Germans become so " raffish "? Why would burglars follow people coming to buy cannabis? And for goodness sake, don’t tell the Journal editors, but prostitution is legal in The Netherlands, so they don’t need pimps.)

The hope is that the drive-thrus will, like the Pied Piper of Hamelin, draw all the rats out of town. But the story of the Pied Piper does not have a happy ending and neither, we suspect, will this one. Recall that the piper ultimately got rid of the rats by leading them to the river where they drowned. Presumably the Venlo city council does not propose to do the same with the drug tourists, meaning (at best) that they'll simply move into somebody else's backyard.
(MarijuanaNews note: Actually, they will just go home, which is the idea.)

Recall, too, that the piper, in revenge for having not been paid, piped the town's children to the mountain, from which they were never heard from again.
(MarijuanaNews note: It is the Journal editors who are refusing to count the costs of their policies and it is DEAland that is losing its children, not the Dutch. The average age of Dutch heroin addicts is almost twice that of those in DEAland, where there are more and more children using heroin.)
See
The Spin Is Beginning To Wobble On The " Latest Teen Drug Use " Survey. Czar Is " Greatly Encouraged " By Poll Showing Heroin Use By 12th Graders At All Time High.

We won't abuse this fable any longer except to note that the Netherlands registered a 250% increase in adolescent marijuana use following the liberalization of its drug laws in the 1980s.

MarijuanaNews note: There are four things wrong with this statement. First, Dutch cannabis policies were " liberalized " in 1976, not the 1980s. Second, it ignores the fact that marijuana use has increased all over the world, not just in The Netherlands. Third, even after this purported increase, Dutch teen marijuana use is still lower than that of DEAland and many other European countries that arrest marijuana users.

" Since 1969 there have been over a dozen surveys on drug use in the Netherlands, two of which offer support for (this) claim. One 1984 survey found that 4.4% of Dutch youth had tried cannabis, while a different 1992 survey by the Dutch National Institute on Alcohol and Drugs (NIAD) found that 10.6% had done so. However, prevalence figures in the other surveys varied widely. As NIAD itself admits, most of the surveys used different samples and methods, which may make their findings non-comparable from year to year. The only survey on drug use which employs rigorously comparable sampling and methods each time it is administered is funded by the Dutch Ministry of Health and conducted on the general population of Amsterdam (the city with the highest concentration of coffeeshops). These surveys found that the proportion of youth aged 12-15 who had ever tried cannabis was 4.7% in 1987, 2.9% in 1990, and 5.8% in 1994. Among youth aged 16-19, the figures were 25.5% in 1987, 21.7% in 1990, and 28.7% in 1994. Rather than a " 200% " jump in cannabis use, these surveys show first a modest decline in lifetime prevalence and four years hence a modest increase. "

With the Venlo scheme, any teenager who can see above the dashboard of daddy's car may purchase drugs without much being done to verify his age. We only hope it won't occur to the boys and girls to get high on the road and forget to buckle their seatbelts.
(MarijuanaNews note: Most Dutch teenagers don’t drive until they are 18, so that shouldn’t be a problem. Of course, coffee-shops get in trouble for selling to anyone under 18 so they do check IDs. The Dutch generally regret raising the minimum age from 16 to 18, but there is pressure from other countries.)

Nor is the Venlo plan likely to get rid of the town's really criminal types. Those who frequent Venlo to get the harder stuff will keep coming, since they probably already know a dealer and don't want to go through the hassle of finding a new one elsewhere. And what's to keep the drive-thru customers from buying drugs and then coming to town?
(MarijuanaNews note: It seems that the Journal’s complaint is that this will not solve all the world’s problems. There will continue to be tooth decay, etc.)

From what we can tell, the Venlo plan makes no provision for a drawbridge and moat.

Defenders of current drug laws in Holland argue that the social problems associated with liberalization are the fault of outsiders who abuse the system, not the Dutch themselves. Thus the vast increases in heroin addiction, property crime, gun-related deaths, organized criminal activity, and the consequent need for one of the largest police forces in the world--all that, it's argued, could be solved if every other country in the world adopted enlightened Dutch ways.
(MarijuanaNews note: What " vast increases in heroin addiction "? Lifetime prevalence of heroin use (ages 12+) in The Netherlands is 0.3%. In DEAland it is 1.1%, almost four times the Dutch rate!

What gun-related deaths? The DEAland murder rate is also over four times the Dutch rate.

As for comparison of the size of police forces, this is of dubious relevance, but the Dutch per capita spending on drug-related law enforcement is $27 versus $81 in DEAland. Incarceration rate per 100,000 population is 73 in The Netherlands versus 645 in DEAland.

I suspect that the Journal editors got some of these bogus number from the shameful 1999 article in Foreign Affairs, which was also used by McCaffrey to lie about the Dutch.)

Maybe. But until the rest of the world goes Dutch, the Dutch will have a problem. Legalization may reduce the incentive for drug-related crime, but it also vastly increases the number of users, a significant point given that 80% of violent crime in the U.S. is committed by people under the influence of some form of intoxicant.
(MarijuanaNews note: Since this is mostly alcohol, and very little of it is cannabis, it is hard to see the relevance of this point.)

And this is all the more true if only marijuana is decriminalized, as the consequences of looser social restrictions and more drug-influenced behavior are not even partly offset by a decrease in heroin- and cocaine-use-related crime.
(MarijuanaNews note: This is also not borne out by the Dutch data. And other " drugs " are not " legal " in The Netherlands, so this is also irrelevant.)

In fact, the more we think about it, the more it seems to us that the drive-thru idea is so dumb it could only have occurred to someone completely stoned. We trust the good citizens of Venlo are sober enough to notice.
(MarijuanaNews note: Speaking of sober, drive through liquor stores are very common in DEAland, but that does not seem to bother the editors of the Wall Street journal, who are too busy making snide and ignorant comments about a country that does better on virtually every measure of social performance than DEAland.)
See
Legalize Marijuana and Improve High-School Academic Performance? Holland Ranks First –The US Very Low
